chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
title: Hawkins refusing Body and Soul; playing the same hits nightly
summary: Dance and Caldwell discuss how musicians tire of audience requests for their hits, such as Hawkins and Body and Soul or Hodges and Carney.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: But, of course, the only thing is that I think, you know, like when Hawk used to be playing at Metropola the Metropolitan, you know, night after night after night, and I mean the man has already been playing for 40 years, and they get up and played the same numbers. Well, I mean a lot of nights that solo is just going to come out very much the same.
It's true.
Because you can't -- I mean you can't think fresh on the same number night after night.
Definitely, no. You're right.
The only thing would be, I guess, if you, you know, if Roy played something extra special, you had better pull out something too.

That's right. Now, I went down to the Metropole -- I went down to see Hawk. And we went downstairs talking, drinking, and people came down and requested 'Body and Soul'. He wouldn't play it. So I -- of course, with me, I'd love to hear him play it, you know. But it's like you stated. You play it every night.
I know, something goes out of it.
It does. That's true.
On top of that, the trouble is when you make a hit record like (unintelligible), and then they want to hear it played like you did on the record.
That's right.
Well, you know, that's awful.
Very awful. That's true. Hawk wouldn't play it. They say, Hawk, you won't play this? Every night they request it. I said, I understand how you feel, said, I don't blame you.
Well, I think a lot of people
That sort of thing

forget, you know, like (unintelligible), you take -- I mean that's one example, but then you take Johnny Hodges with two. Well, I mean he was playing -- he was playing "Things Ain't What They Used to Be" for 35 years practically every night of his life.
That's true.

Harry Carey played "Sophisticated Lady" every night of his life -- I mean all you could really expect then is they go through the motions, and they produce a nice tone, but you can't expect them to --
Definitely not. If he wanted to change what he wanted to play on it, he couldn't because --
I'll (Unintelligible).

Forever, that's right. That's true. That's very true. The old master spoke (unintelligible) Hawk, but he said he didn't want to play "Body and Soul." He told me Hop Me (unintelligible) and I said, Bean, you know what you want to do. I said, I understand how you feel and I don't blame you for that.
Well, I know that, you know, you can -- that was one thing that you did want to hear him play (unintelligible) --
(Laughter)

-- I know, but the second time, you know, he -- he played so many beautiful ballads, you know. He -- I made an album with him and Buck Clayton, and, you know, so he said, well, what do you want me to play? I said, you play what you want. Now,
"You've" he came and he played whole Changed.
That's beautiful.
